_comment: Mutation testing asks the question coverage cannot: not whether a line ran, but whether the
tests would NOTICE if it were wrong. A line can be covered by a test that asserts nothing.
Scope is deliberate, not lazy. Mutating 65,000 lines would take hours and produce a number
nobody acts on. These five areas are where a surviving mutant is a real defect waiting to
happen - authentication, the HTTP interceptor chain, consent, legal acceptance and user
preferences - and every one of them has specs already. Components are mostly template binding,
where a surviving mutant usually means a snapshot moved rather than behaviour broke.
Two settings here are not preferences, they are the price of running Stryker against an
Angular project at all. Both cost an afternoon to find, so they are written down:
inPlace  Stryker's jest runner reads `configFile` from the real project, so `<rootDir>` in
our testMatch resolves to the real project - but it runs jest with `roots` pointing
at the sandbox copy. The two never intersect and jest reports `No tests were found`,
which looks like a config error and is not one. Mutating in place is the escape
Stryker documents for projects that depend on file locations. CI checks out fresh,
so it costs nothing there; locally Stryker restores from .stryker-tmp/backup-* .
jsdom    jest.config.js states `testEnvironment: 'jsdom'` explicitly. Stryker reads the
resolved config without expanding the preset, defaults to node, and then every
Angular spec dies on `window is not defined`.
`break` stays null on purpose: the floor is enforced by tools/ci/mutation-summary.mjs instead,
so a run below the floor still publishes its report and still tells you WHICH mutants lived.
Stryker breaking the build first would take the report down with it.
First measurement (2026-09-10, 486 mutants over 18 files): 72.84 % overall, 83.29 % on covered
code. The floor in the workflow sits at 70 - a ratchet, raised when the score rises, never
lowered to make a red run green.
